articles.title: Study traces how an El Niño changed the pollution map
articles.summary: The winter of 2022-23 was remarkably clean in north India with PM2.5 levels down by up to 30% from the average of the previous three years, while
articles.body: The winter of 2022-23 was remarkably clean in north India with PM2.5 levels down by up to 30% from the average of the previous three years, while peninsular India was considerably dirtier, with average PM2.5 levels in Mumbai spiking by 45%. The next winter (2023-24), the pattern dramatically reversed: PM2.5 spiralled in the North, while falling sharply in peninsular India.What changed within a span of a year? The big difference, as per a new study, was that 2022-23 was a La Niña year, while El Niño prevailed in the subsequent winter.Coming ahead of India’s peak pollution season, the paper, titled ‘Air quality in flux: The baffling ENSO transition in India’, published in Atmospheric Pollution Research journal Thursday, found that La Niña/El Niño conditions altered atmospheric circulation, PM2.5 transport pathways and weather conditions that determine whether pollution disperses or gets trapped.That atmospheric conditions regulate pollution levels was always known. What the study shows is how the atmosphere in winters can behave very differently under El Nino and La Nina conditions, determining where pollutants accumulate and where they are carried away even when emissions remain broadly similar. However, the researchers caution that the study does not establish that El Niño invariably worsens air quality in Delhi or north India.“We are not implying that the 2023-24 El Niño pattern will be repeated this winter. The two years that we studied were unusual and unique,” said atmospheric scientist Gufran Beig, one of the study’s authors. “This year’s El Niño is likely to be the strongest on record.”The study found that during the La Niña winter of 2022-23, stronger winds over north India helped disperse emissions from stubble-burning and local sources. The altered circulation bypassed Delhi and its surroundings and transported these pollutants southwards towards peninsular India. This resulted in substantially higher PM2.5 levels in cities such as Mumbai and Thiruvananthapuram.The following winter, the atmospheric setup changed. Under El Niño, winds over northern India were weaker and passed through areas, including Delhi and Jaipur, rather than carrying pollutants away. The resulting stagnation favoured the accumulation of PM2.5. Jaipur, for instance, recorded an increase of about 50% compared with the 2019-22 average, while Delhi logged a spike of over 10%.Weather conditions also mattered differently in the two years. Rain can remove pollutants from air, while high pressure, weak winds and a shallow boundary layer can trap them close to the ground. In Jaipur, rainfall was more strongly associated with lower PM2.5 during 2022-23, whereas surface pressure became a more important factor during 2023-24, leading to pollution spikes after rain.The researchers also used backward air-mass trajectories to trace where the air reaching cities had travelled from. Jaipur continued to receive air from polluted northern regions during the El Niño winter. Hyderabad, by contrast, received more marine and southern air, helping explain why its pollution pattern moved in the opposite direction.Overall, the study found substantial year-to-year PM2.5 variations from average levels in 2019-22 — ranging from about a 40% decline to a 70% increase, despite no major changes in emissions or pollution-control policies during the period. The authors underlined that the correlations neither establish direct causation nor can these be extrapolated to other years.For Delhi-NCR, this has an important implication: relatively low local or agricultural emissions do not automatically guarantee cleaner air if large-scale circulation turns stagnant. Conversely, even substantial emissions can have a smaller local impact when strong winds efficiently disperse or divert them.The winter pollution story may begin in Delhi and its neighbourhood, but increasingly, the weather that decides its intensity is being written on a much larger canvas.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Freed US citizen Stephen Hubbard was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
articles.summary: Ukrainians held alongside the American say they witnessed beatings and sexual humiliation by Russian guards during his detention.
articles.body:
Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.

Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.

"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."

Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.

"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."

Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.

He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.

Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.

"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.

"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."

Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.

Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.

The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.

Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.

Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.

He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.

Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.

"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.

Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.

"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.

"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."

They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.

"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.

Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.

"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."

Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.

He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.

"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".

Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.

"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.

But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".

Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.

"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".

articles.title: In 2024, interior designers paid $3.874 million for Bob Barker's historic 1929 Los Angeles mansion; after an extensive renovation, the 5,906-square-foot home sold in April 2026 for $6.325 million
articles.summary: A historic Hollywood Hills home once owned by longtime 'The Price Is Right' host Bob Barker has changed hands again, this time after an extensive
articles.body: A historic Hollywood Hills home once owned by longtime 'The Price Is Right' host Bob Barker has changed hands again, this time after an extensive restoration by interior designer Julia Dempster. The 1929 Spanish Colonial Revival estate at 1851 Outpost Drive was bought by Dempster in April 2024 for $3.874 million, according to Mansion Global. After a renovation that preserved original architectural details while modernising key parts of the house, the 5,906-square-foot property sold in April 2026 for $6.325 million, according to public sale records and real estate listings.The sale marks a notable chapter for one of Outpost Estates’ most storied properties. Barker purchased the home in 1969 and lived there for more than five decades until his death in 2023, while the land beneath it is tied to Hollywood’s earliest residential history. The renovation did not simply refresh the interiors; it aimed to make a nearly century-old house functional for contemporary living without erasing the character that made it distinctive.A home with Hollywood historyThe property sits in Outpost Estates, an enclave in the Hollywood Hills known for its early Los Angeles history and celebrity residents. The current house was completed in 1929 on the site of what has been described as Hollywood’s original adobe home. Before Barker, the estate was associated with Los Angeles Times publisher General Harrison Gray Otis and developer Charles E. Toberman, who helped shape parts of early Hollywood, as per the reports.Barker acquired the Spanish Revival residence in 1969 and made it his primary home for more than 50 years. The late television host, who won 19 Emmy Awards and was known for his animal-rights advocacy, lived there until his death in August 2023, shortly before his 100th birthday. His long ownership gave the house a personal history that extended far beyond its architectural value.When the home first came to market after Barker’s death, it was presented as a restoration opportunity. Robb Report reported that the property retained original stained-glass windows, wrought-iron detailing, antique light fixtures and a delicate fresco on the wood-beamed ceiling above the switchback staircase. The house needed updating, but it also carried rare period features that made a sensitive renovation especially important.Julia Dempster’s renovationDempster, a London-based interior designer, purchased the home in April 2024 for $3.784 million, according to Cottages and Gardens, which cited Mansion Global. The reported price was $800,000 above asking, reflecting competition for a property with both historic significance and strong potential in one of Los Angeles’ desirable hillside neighbourhoods.Her renovation focused on restoring rather than replacing the home’s original character. The project included modifying the original ironwork balustrade, preserving and replacing wood floors, restoring original doors and applying Portola Roman clay to the walls. Dempster also modernised the bathrooms, redid the clay-tile roof and carried out other work intended to bring the 1929 residence up to modern standards.The result was a five-bedroom, seven-bathroom home with 5,906 square feet of interior space. Listing details describe beamed, coffered and tray ceilings, crown mouldings, stained or leaded windows, wood flooring, a family room with a fireplace, an office and a kitchen with granite counters, an island and a breakfast area. The house also includes indoor laundry, multiple patios and a primary suite with a walk-in closet.From $3.874 million to $6.325 millionThe property’s recent sales history shows how much the renovation changed its market position. Realtor.com’s property history records an April 25, 2024 sale at $3.788 million, or $641 per square foot. The home returned to market in June 2025 at $8.195 million, a jump of more than 116 percent from its previous sale price, before the asking price was reduced to $7.798 million in July 2025.The final sale did not reach the original asking price, but it still represented a substantial increase from the 2024 purchase. Public records and market reports show the home sold for $6.325 million on April 30, 2026, with the transaction recorded around April 29. That is roughly $2.45 million above the price Dempster paid in 2024, although the final figure excludes renovation costs, selling expenses and the time involved in the project.The Outpost Neighborhood Association noted that the estate ultimately sold for $6.325 million after debuting at $8.195 million in June 2025. It described the outcome as evidence of how important pricing alignment has become in the current market, even for homes with strong history and high-end finishes.A new owner with a connection to Hollywood magicThe buyer was reported as Randy Pitchford, the video-game executive and magician who owns Los Angeles’ historic Magic Castle. Mansion Global reported that Pitchford and his wife, Kristy, bought the former Barker home for $6.235 million, while other property records and market reports list the final sale price as $6.325 million. The slight difference appears to reflect reporting variations or transaction details, but both accounts identify the buyer as Pitchford and place the sale in spring 2026.For Pitchford, the purchase adds another piece of Hollywood heritage to a portfolio already connected to the city’s entertainment history. The Magic Castle, located in the Hollywood Hills, is a private club for magicians and magic enthusiasts, while 1851 Outpost Drive carries its own links to early Hollywood and television history.Why the renovation matteredThe story of 1851 Outpost Drive shows how a well-executed restoration can add value without treating history as an obstacle. Dempster preserved original doors, floors, ironwork and other period elements while updating bathrooms, roofing and finishes for present-day comfort. That balance helped the home appeal to buyers seeking both character and practicality.It also demonstrates that celebrity history alone does not guarantee a sale at any price. The home initially listed above $8 million, was reduced and eventually sold for $6.325 million. Yet the property still achieved a strong outcome relative to its 2024 purchase price, supported by its rare provenance, restored condition and location in Outpost Estates.For Los Angeles real estate watchers, the sale is a reminder that the most valuable homes are often those with a clear story. In this case, the story included Hollywood’s first adobe site, Bob Barker’s five-decade residence and a designer-led renovation that gave a 1929 Spanish Colonial Revival a carefully updated second life.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Laid off on H-1B, 1 interview after 100 applications: Redditor shares harrowing job situation in US
articles.summary: A Redditor who has been laid off in the US took to social media and explained the harrowing ground situation. \"Every single day since then was like hell.
articles.body: A Redditor who has been laid off in the US took to social media and explained the harrowing ground situation. "Every single day since then was like hell. I have been in the US for 8 years and all of a sudden I lost everything I have," the Redditor said, adding that there was no warning before the layoff. it was just a normal day and suddenly the job was not there anymore. "The company even refused to put me on the payrolls to maintain my H1b status, said too much legal complications but gave me a severance package instead," the Reddit post said."I tried to apply for jobs like no tomorrows and had 100 applications and 1 interview so far after a week. I had friends to give me referrals everywhere but most didn't help," the Redditor said.The post made it clear that the employee asked the company to be kept on the payroll so that they could maintain H-1B status while looking for another job. But the company apparently refused to do so for legal complications, possibly jeopardizing the Redditor's immigration status.The worker may qualify for a grace period of up to 60 consecutive days, or until the end of the authorised validity period, whichever comes first. During that period, they can look for another sponsoring employer. If an eligible new employer properly files a qualifying H-1B petition, the worker may generally begin working under the portability rules without waiting for approval. The grace period is discretionary, not guaranteed.But as explained in the Reddit post, 100 applications come with one interview making the job search tough for a laid-off H-1B visa holder.'Go back home'The comment section was full of vitriol, reminding the Redditor that those jobs were never meant for foreigners in the first place. Though the Redditor did not mention nationality, many people asked the individual to 'go back to India'.What happens when an H-1B visa holder is laid off?If an H-1B worker is laid off and cannot find another job before their grace period expires, they do have options, but they may have to change their immigration status, leave the US, or find another lawful way to remain. After eight years in the US, as the Redditor described, this can be especially difficult because their job, housing, family plans and long-term green-card process may all be affected.1. Find another H-1B sponsoring employerA new employer can file an H-1B petition. Eligible workers can generally start working once the new petition is properly filed, under H-1B portability rules. The new employer must be willing and eligible to sponsor them.2. Change to a dependent visa, such as H-4 or L-2If their spouse qualifies under the relevant visa category, they may be able to change status to become a dependent. Work authorisation is a separate question: for example, only certain H-4 spouses qualify for an employment authorisation document, while eligible L-2 spouses may have work authorisation incident to status.3. Change to student status (F-1)They could consider enrolling in a genuine qualifying academic programme and applying to change status. This is not a way to keep working freely: they generally cannot begin employment unless separately authorised, and any student work must comply with the applicable rules.4. Apply to change status to B-2 visitorThis may allow them to remain temporarily in the US while arranging their affairs or exploring their options, if USCIS approves the application. But they cannot work on B-2 status, including taking up ordinary paid employment while waiting for a new job. A timely, non-frivolous application may allow an authorised period of stay while it is pending, but it does not itself grant work authorisation.5. Explore a green-card-related optionSomeone with an employment-based green-card case may have additional possibilities, depending on their circumstances. For instance, certain workers with a qualifying I-140 petition and a pending I-485 for at least 180 days may be able to transfer the green-card job offer to a new employer in the same or a similar occupational classification. A separate, discretionary employment authorisation for compelling circumstances may also be available to some eligible applicants. Neither route is automatic.6. Leave the US and pursue a job from abroadIf no viable status option exists, they may have to leave the US. They can continue applying for American jobs from their home country, and a prospective employer may be able to sponsor a new H-1B petition if they qualify. They should check their remaining H-1B time and any applicable cap requirements before making plans. An employer that involuntarily terminates an H-1B worker generally must offer to pay reasonable transportation costs to the worker's last place of foreign residence.You use AI every day. articles.body: Slack co-founder Stewart Butterfield and Away co-founder Jen Rubio have sold their sprawling Aspen, Colorado, estate for $30 million, closing a significant real estate deal just weeks after announcing their separation. Despite the timing, the sale was not linked to the couple’s separation, according to a spokesperson cited by The Wall Street Journal. Another notable transaction involved their Tribeca townhouse, connected by a distinctive skybridge, which sold for $24 million that year.Butterfield co-founded Slack, the workplace messaging platform that was acquired by Salesforce in 2021 for $27.7 billion. articles.title: This Arkansas mining town reached 3,000 people during the World War I zinc boom; by 1920, its population had plunged to 344
articles.summary: Rush, Arkansas, grew from a zinc mining settlement into a community of up to 3,000 residents during the mining boom associated with the First World War.
articles.body: Rush, Arkansas, grew from a zinc mining settlement into a community of up to 3,000 residents during the mining boom associated with the First World War. Rising demand for zinc, used in brass for weapons and ammunition, helped drive production at Rush Mountain between 1911 and 1918. However, the boom was short-lived. After the war, falling zinc prices forced mines to close, and the town’s population dropped to 344 by 1920. Mining eventually ended at the Morning Star Mine in 1931, but remnants of the industry, including abandoned mines, buildings and mill ruins, remain within the Rush Historic District along the Buffalo River.How did Rush, Arkansas, transport zinc oreAs mining operations grew, Rush developed into a community that supported the workforce. According to the NPS, the town expanded to include offices, hotels, barns, shops, a courthouse and a post office. Mills were constructed where mining companies worked through the richest zinc deposits. These facilities processed the extracted ore, separating valuable minerals from waste before the material was transported onwards.The mining district also developed its own transport infrastructure. The NPS explains that elevated tramways carried ore from mines on the hillsides to mills below. However, transporting zinc beyond Rush presented a significant challenge because the Buffalo River was not deep enough for ore boats and no railways were located close to the settlement. Miners relied on horse and mule teams to haul the ore along rough dirt roads to Summit, the nearest railway access, or to Old Buffalo City, where it could be loaded onto a barge and floated to Batesville on the White River.Why did Rush, Arkansas, decline after the zinc mining boomAt the height of its mining activity, Rush’s population ranged from 2,000 to 3,000 residents, according to the NPS’s account of the Rush Historic District. The community’s growth was closely linked to zinc production and the demand generated by the First World War. The district’s mines and supporting businesses attracted workers, while advertisements promoted the possibility of making a fortune in the mining settlement.The boom did not last. The NPS records that the wartime period of increased zinc sales ended in 1918, followed by a decline in production in 1919. By 1920, Rush had only 344 residents. An excess supply of zinc after the war drove prices down, forcing many mines to close. The Morning Star Mine, the district’s largest mining operation, eventually shut in 1931, marking the end of the mining era associated with the historic district.What remains of Rush, Arkansas’s historic mining districtAlthough mining operations ended, physical evidence of Rush’s industrial past remains within the Rush Historic District, which lies inside the Buffalo National River in Boone County, Arkansas. The NPS identifies surviving features including the Taylor-Medley General Store, Rush Blacksmith Shop, Rush Smelter, former residences and several mines and tunnels. Some of the underground mining features are visible from the surface, although they have been fenced off or otherwise closed.The remains also include deteriorating houses and the ruins of the Morning Star Hotel and Mill, alongside archaeological sites associated with the former community. Vegetation has grown around some structures, while flooding and arson have damaged or destroyed other historic features over the years. The Rush Historic District was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1987.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trans rights support gets me daily abuse, says Doctor Who writer Russell T Davies
articles.summary: The Doctor Who writer says his latest mini-series TipToe has fuelled daily hate messages online.
articles.body:
Screenwriter Russell T Davies has said he gets called a "groomer" and a "paedophile" every day by online trolls over his support of transgender rights.

The Doctor Who writer said comments were fuelled by his latest mini series TipToe, which focuses on a feud between neighbours on opposite ends of the political debate.

Davies described it as a reflection of "real world issues" he felt necessary to speak up on and admitted he now has agents who monitor his hate "every day".

"I think the rise of the online voice, the voice of anger, which is becoming more homophobic and misogynist and anti-Semitic and every problem you could name, is stepping out of the online world into the real world," he said.

"I genuinely think there are dangers out there... that's the story of TipToe, every prejudice and problem arriving at your front door.

"I'm very safe, I'm well off, nicely paid, I'm a white man, I have support around me... but it makes me sick to think what is it like to be a young, trans kid, living in a flat and working in a bar, not a penny to you.

"If you feel afraid, that's terrifying. And I've had people say that to me, I've had trans people say that to my face."

Trans rights and gender identity remains a heated political debate that has incited violent behaviour towards people on both sides of the argument.

Harry Potter author JK Rowling has had extensive criticism for a series of comments voicing concerns about how trans issues affect women's rights, and her opposition to Scotland's gender recognition bill .

In 2024, an internet troll was handed two suspended sentences after posting "chilling" online messages threatening to kill Rowling and former MP Rosie Duffield, who is known for her critical stance on transgender self‑identification.

Davies said he's fearful for the growing harmfulness of social media.

"I have hope because I think people are marvellous but I see absolutely no signs of the technology being reined in or controlled," he said.

"And if that is going to happen, there has to be a revolution... but I don't see any signs of a revolution because we are all busy scrolling."

The 63-year-old was speaking to Jo Whiley on a BBC Radio 2 podcast about his new memoir, The Queerest of Folk, which follows his life and career in television, including bringing queer stories to the mainstream.

The Swansea-born writer started out in Youth theatre before his TV career began with the BBC Children's department.

His breakthrough came from drama Queer as Folk, first aired in 1999, and regarded as a turning point for on-screen LGBTQ+ representation .

It depicted three characters living in Manchester's gay village and was explicit in a way that had not been seen on UK TV before.

Davies said he still gets "extraordinary" responses more than 26 years later: "I get people who walk up to me in Manchester to say I've only moved up here because of Queer as Folk... it's very moving, it's very powerful."

Despite being faced with criticism for his work, Davies said he always wants to remain true to himself and what he believes in as it is "all that matters".

Tonia Antonazzi, a Labour MP who has been vocal about her views on protecting female-only spaces , said she had witnessed the backlash Davies had experienced and felt for him.

"I hugely respect Russell. He's been a fantastic advocate for gender rights," she said, adding that she believed Davies himself would not want to diminish anyone's rights.

"We must not lose sex-based rights. Many women feel silenced, that they cannot say they need to have women-only spaces."

She said self identification is important for single-sex spaces, sport, and changing rooms and also noted the importance of gender for data collection across public bodies.

But Antoniazzi believes the conversation around gender identity needed to be an open one, without the threat of hatred or harm to either side and "shouldn't be an us-versus-them".

She admitted that putting her head above the parapet made her susceptible to hate online, including death threats.

"I ignore it rather than be a victim to it... as a female MP, I don't want to be silenced."

In 2024, a tweet posted by the Gower MP went viral and resulted in her being a target for hate, "from people within my own party", she said.

She has now turned off comments on her Facebook page "because of foul comments" and said it was done to protect the well-being of her family, friends and staff.

"The threat is real," said Antoniazzi, alluding to the death of former Tory MP Anne Widdecombe , adding that she is "super careful" about what she does.

"I do have to plan ahead... I'm content in my small town, but other areas in my constituency I do sometimes think 'I'm not going there by myself' and I have to think about the security and staff I have with me."

articles.title: Ukrainian soldier cuts off his own foot to survive, rescued by drone after 8 months
articles.summary: A Ukrainian soldier who spent nearly eight months trapped in a bombed-out school has been rescued from the frontline by a heavy-lift drone, in what
articles.body: A Ukrainian soldier who spent nearly eight months trapped in a bombed-out school has been rescued from the frontline by a heavy-lift drone, in what Ukrainian commanders described as the first known aerial drone rescue of a soldier.Kostiantyn Vlasenko, 49, had been stranded in a boiler room with severe injuries after a Russian drone strike. With no way to escape and little hope of being rescued, he made a desperate decision to amputate his remaining foot to survive.On October 4, a large drone lifted him into the air using a harness and carried him 15km to safety. The operation ended an ordeal that had kept him on Ukraine’s drone-infested frontlines for 491 days.The Ukrainian military corroborated Vlasenko’s account, although some details could not be independently verified.A desperate fight to surviveVlasenko was sent to a frontline position in May last year to join a fellow soldier known by the call sign Basky. The two men lived in a cramped dugout and depended on daily drone deliveries for supplies.When the time came to rotate troops in autumn, two soldiers sent to relieve them were killed on their way to the position, Vlasenko said. Two more soldiers sent to recover their bodies also died.After spending 10 months together, Vlasenko and Basky were forced to take shelter in a ruined school when their foxhole flooded in mid-February. Their refuge was soon struck by a Russian drone. Basky was killed on his 50th birthday, while Vlasenko suffered devastating injuries.The strike destroyed his left foot and severely damaged his right leg, leaving him barely able to move. He took shelter beneath the school's boiler, where his condition continued to deteriorate.His right leg was broken, with the bone protruding through the injury. Unable to move properly and fearing he would not survive, he eventually used a knife to amputate his remaining foot and applied a tourniquet to stop the bleeding.“I had to amputate it because it was just dragging along behind me,” he said. “The leg was dragging so much that the bone was sticking out. So I no longer had either of my legs.”Looking back on his ordeal, Vlasenko told Reuters from his hospital bed in Kharkiv, “I had already buried myself,” adding, “I knew there was no hope left.”Why conventional rescue missions failedRescuing wounded soldiers from the area had become extremely dangerous because Russian drones could target vehicles moving towards the frontline.According to the officer overseeing the operation, who identified himself only by the call sign Alex, evacuations using pickup trucks and armoured vehicles had become almost impossible.Ukrainian forces also tried using unmanned ground vehicles that travelled on wheels or tracks. However, two vehicles sent to reach Vlasenko were destroyed by drones.The officers then learned about a heavy-lift drone being developed by the Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defense. Its six vertical rotors and black frame gave it the appearance of a giant insect. It could carry loads weighing up to 90kg over distances of up to 25km.The officers estimated that Vlasenko weighed around 70kg after spending more than a year at the frontline. The drone would have to transport him approximately 15km to reach safety.The mission remained dangerous because larger Ukrainian drones could be intercepted by smaller Russian first-person-view drones. These allow remote operators to see what the drone sees in real time and guide it towards its target.Suspended beneath a droneIn early October, Vlasenko received an unusual delivery among his regular supply parcels. It contained a harness and a phone with instructional videos explaining how to use it.The following day, October 4, the heavy-lift drone arrived. Vlasenko attached himself to a carabiner connected to a winch beneath the aircraft. The machine then lifted him to a height of 70 metres and began carrying him away from the frontline.Three smaller six-propeller drones accompanied the aircraft to distract Russian attack drones. Meanwhile, four Ukrainian first-person-view drone crews, artillery units and larger fixed-wing drones attacked known Russian drone positions for two hours to suppress enemy fire.After a tense 15-minute journey, the drone reached its destination and landed safely.Vlasenko said he had worried about falling during the flight, particularly into water because he could not swim.“I wasn’t afraid of falling, say into the forest,” he said. “But I was afraid of falling into the water, because I can’t swim,” he said.The rescue demonstrated how Ukraine is increasingly relying on unmanned aircraft not only to deliver supplies and attack enemy positions, but also to evacuate wounded soldiers from areas where conventional rescue vehicles cannot safely operate.You use AI every day. articles.title: An LA advertising couple bought a $925,000 California farm with no house, turned its barn loft into a home for $100,000, and built an apple orchard and cider business into a family destination
articles.summary: David Bailey, 40, and Dana Tiel were advertising professionals in Los Angeles before deciding to trade city life for a different kind of challenge.
articles.body: David Bailey, 40, and Dana Tiel were advertising professionals in Los Angeles before deciding to trade city life for a different kind of challenge. Their growing interest in gardening got them thinking about farming. Before they knew it, they had their eyes set on a 16-acre farm in Mariposa, California, with a four-acre apple orchard and an established hard cider business. They purchased the property for $925,000, despite there being no house on the land. They spent another $100,000 converting the barn loft into a home. Their curiosity project has now grown into Sierra Cider, a family destination offering cider tastings, a petting zoo, a seasonal pumpkin patch and a pick-your-own apple orchard.Where a pastime search endedThe couple started looking for properties as a pastime. For about three months, they sent each other listings during the workday, ruling out anything above 500 acres. Then, on the drive back from visiting Dana’s mother in Oregon, they passed an orange grove. ‘I think what we want is a citrus grove or apple orchard,’ she told her husband, as reported by Realtor.com. She changed the search that afternoon and found the Mariposa listing within minutes. The property was right next to Yosemite."My wife and I had always dreamed of living on a farm someday, so when the pandemic hit and we were cooped up in our house in LA, we decided to make the most insane COVID purchase imaginable. When we found this 800-tree farm with a business attached to it, it was the perfect opportunity to not only learn new skills but also use our experience as advertising creatives to build the brand," David told Collabs.io Mag.The seller was offering a turnkey hard cider business, with the equipment included. The couple wondered what the catch was. It turned out to be the lack of a house.The asking price for the property was $1.25 million. The couple felt it was too high for a property with no living space. They made an offer and eventually settled at $925,000. They skipped a USDA loan and borrowed from an agricultural lender that specialises in small businesses. The loan carries an adjustable interest rate, a detail they accepted with their eyes open.Turning a hayloft into a homeBuying the property was only the beginning. The challenge was about to start. The couple, of course, needed a place to live. The barn had a loft that could be converted into a one-bedroom apartment. The previous owners had always intended the space to become living quarters, so gas and plumbing lines already reached it. That saved time, but the renovation still took seven months and cost about $100,000.Living on site during the work was harder than they expected, however. They stayed in Airbnbs for two months before moving into a camper for another five. All this time, the couple were still working full-time in advertising while learning to run a farm and a small business. It was not easy. Bailey admitted that they questioned the decision almost every day.People around them were also concerned. Bailey’s parents strongly opposed the purchase, and his uncle, who also serves as their accountant, did the same. This only made things worse for them. They considered backing out several times but decided they would regret not taking the chance more.A destination farmToday, the property operates as Sierra Cider. The tasting room is open from Friday to Sunday, and the grounds include a petting zoo, a seasonal pumpkin patch and a pick-your-own orchard that runs from August through October. People can sit and enjoy their cider while their children play in the fenced compound. The farm also hosts summer camps for children.The orchard grows many varieties of apples, mostly cider apples. The harvest season starts in July, and Bailey’s favourite part remains the picking itself. ‘To be on a ladder picking apples, there is nothing better,’ he told the outlet.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: ‘A racist terror attack’: French President Macron condemns deadly shooting near Paris
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron called a shooting spree in the Paris suburbs as \"a racist terror attack\", saying the victims were targeted because of
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron called a shooting spree in the Paris suburbs as "a racist terror attack", saying the victims were targeted because of their skin colour or perceived religion. One person was killed and at least five others, including a 12-year-old girl, were injured in the attacks.The gunman opened fire at three locations in Trappes and La Verrière, about 30 kilometres west of Paris, over a period of around 15 minutes, French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said. Three of the injured suffered life-threatening injuries."These people were targeted because of their skin colour or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Macron said after meeting officials and residents in Trappes. "There is no place for this in France."Macron also said the suspect's statements indicated that the attack had been planned in advance.Suspect arrested within 20 minutesPolice arrested the suspect less than 20 minutes after the shooting began. France's National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's office has taken charge of the investigation.The suspect has been identified as Kévin T, born in 1987. Authorities have not released his full surname. He had four previous convictions, which had been automatically expunged under French law, the prosecutor's office said.Investigators found a Sten-type submachine gun and a canister of tear gas inside his car. A search of his apartment also uncovered three gas cylinders and electrical wires connected to a timer, which authorities said had been arranged as a trap.A member of the suspect's immediate family was also taken into police custody on Friday afternoon.The person killed was a French man born in 2000. The condition of the injured victims had not stabilised by Friday evening, the prosecutor's office said.Nuñez praised the five officers from the anti-crime brigade who stopped the suspect. "I commend them for their swift response," he said.Authorities investigate suspected racist motiveTrappes Mayor Ali Rabeh said the gunman appeared to have fired at passersby at several locations, including a playground. He suggested the victims may have been targeted because of their apparent African origin."This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," he told reporters.Aurore Bergé, France's minister for gender equality and the fight against discrimination, said the 12-year-old girl had been very seriously injured."If a racist motive is established, I hope that the whole nation will stand alongside the residents of Trappes, La Verrière, and the victims. We cannot tolerate even the slightest racist remark in the French Republic," she said.The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's office has opened a criminal investigation into several offences, including "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise with the aggravating circumstance that the act was committed on account of the victim's actual or perceived membership of a particular race, ethnic group, nationality or religion".The attack comes as France prepares for another day of protests against the rising cost of living on Saturday.Authorities have announced tighter security measures following violent unrest last week. Major museums are set to close, while the government plans to deploy a significantly larger security presence to prevent further violence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
